title: Ben Graham & the Growth Investor | Hewitt Heiserman | Talks at Google
description:
Hewitt Heiserman authored "It's Earnings That Count" and is finishing his second book, “The Checklist Investor”. He is a member of the Boston Security Analyst Society and CFA Institute. He has written for several investing publications.. He graduated from Kenyon College and received the Faculty Award for Distinguished Achievement. He is an Ironman finisher, and is active in open land preservation.

The slides to pair with this talk can be found at: https://goo.gl/kg1BtL
summary: The speaker argues that investors should focus on the 200-day moving average as a critical trend indicator, noting that stocks falling below this line often experience significant declines. He contrasts this technical approach with value investing principles, citing Ben Graham's net working capital method and Warren Buffett's long-term franchise assessments. The talk also highlights the volatility of specific companies, illustrating how quickly stocks can collapse after breaking key technical levels.

transcript: MALE SPEAKER: Hello and welcome everyone. We have a very special guest with us here today, Hewitt Heiserman. He authored the book, "It's Earnings That Count," and he is currently finishing his second book, "The Checklist Investor." The interesting thing about today's talk is that he is going to be sharing material which I am told might become his third book. So you guys are the first ones to get a look at it. Mr. Heiserman is a member of the Boston Security Analyst Society and CFA Institute. He's been quoted in various publications including the Wall Street Journal and Barron's. He has spoken to several CFA groups as well as Fidelity Management, Franklin Templeton, and the American Association of Individual Investors. He is, interestingly, an Ironman finisher and is active in open land preservation. Lastly, and I guess more importantly, he is a recipient of the Kenyan College's faculty award for distinguished achievement. And he will be speaking to us wearing his teacher's hat. We are really glad to have you here. Ladies and gentlemen, please join me in welcoming, Hewitt Heiserman. [APPLAUSE] HEWITT HEISERMAN: The title of my talk is Ben Graham and the Growth Investor. And if you know anything about Ben, you know that famously he was a value investor. He wanted to buy companies that were cheap in relation to their corporate net worth. And this may seem like a paradox, but I will explain everything shortly. I want to draw your attention to a study that was done by Jeff Smart, a PhD, a venture capital. And these VC firms, including some here in this area were profiled by their personality type. And then their performance in terms of which companies they were investing in. Again, these are early stage pre-revenue companies, highly speculative, maybe just a couple of people, no assets to speak of. The personality type that performed the best were the airline captains. They averaged almost an 80% IRR on their investments. The airline captain followed a discipline repeatable and explainable process when they were interviewing potential candidates to finance. In other words they were using a checklist approach. And this applies to what I'm going to talk about today. This chart here shows that for the last 30 years, just 25% of the stocks created all the stock market returns. And 75% of the stocks either broke even or they lost money. And this chart shows that one out of five is a big winner. 40% lost money and one out of five is a big loser. So if we can tilt the odds of success in our favor, that's a tremendous advantage. So we're going to be using a checklist approach, which is kind of like a race, where there's a series of hurdles. And in our approach, not every company will reach the finish line. You probably know that airline pilots use checklists. And even a company called Google uses checklists. There's a great book by Atul Gawande called, "The Checklist Manifesto." If you haven't read it, there's a lot of good information in there. So here's our checklist for the growth investor. We're going to go through these five items. We're going to spend a little more time on number one, earnings quality and number five, sell. The three in the middle, we're going to go over a little bit faster. I want to acknowledge the luminaries that have spoken here in this series before me. I've tried to watch every presentation. I've taken notes as I've watched these other individual speakers-- a lot of excellent content. I want to acknowledge the people that have helped me get here. My high school, the Haverford School-- I refer to last year. It had the number one ranked boys lacrosse team in the United States. Kenyon College has more NCAA championships than any school in the United States, with the exception of three California schools-- USC, UCLA, and Stanford. Kenyon was named as having one of the most beautiful campuses in the world according to Forbes. And Chuck Huggins, who was the CEO of See's Candy was a graduate. Charlie Monger, who is the vice chairman at Berkshire Hathaway said that See's was their first high quality company that Berkshire bought and that opened up the door to Coca-Cola. They were able to realize the value of pricing power, competitive advantage, and some of these qualitative things that they really hadn't paid attention to earlier in their partnership. And of course I want to acknowledge John Bogle, the founder and former CEO of the Vanguard Group. Mr. Bogle wrote the forward to my book. If he were here today he'd say three things. Number one, no one knows nothing. That was the advice he first learned when he got in the business in the early 50s. Second, most of us should have most of our money in index funds. And third, his life's motto, press on regardless. When I visited Mr. Bogle last April at the Vanguard headquarters, interestingly enough, Google's historian was on their campus that day. And he had just left Mr. Bogle's office as I was going in. After my book was published, Barron's wrote this article that I wrote about the earnings power chart which we're going to discuss. They also published a letter to the editor that I wrote, in which I said-- this is in December 2004. You had just gone public in August of that year. I said that it was unlikely that Google would make $14 billion dollars of earnings by 2014. Actually I said $10 billion. In fact you made $14.4 billion. So congratulations. I also mention this because five years ago I bought a company that went bankrupt. That was the first time I'd ever bought a company that went bankrupt. The point is that these are my ideas, but it's your money. So I want you to test everything that I say today. I'm finishing a book called, "The Checklist Manifesto," which Miles Thompson at Columbia University Press will publish. That should be available in a year. Just to help you get the lay of the land here, there are six broad reasons why you might buy a company's stock-- yield, growth, the company's cheap in relation to its net assets, people, a special situation like a spin-off, and then other includes short-selling. I'm going to address this second column from the left, growth investing. I think this is the most intuitive of the six approaches or the most human. We plant a tree in our yard and we watch the tree grow and then it has flowers or fruit. Or if we're a parent we have kids and we watch our kids grow up. I think we can all relate to the growth approach. One of the great growth stocks of the last 25 years is Microsoft. If you or your parents were lucky or prescient enough to buy $10,000 in 1990, those shares grew to a million dollars by the end of 1999. Now you can see in these blue bars here-- that's earnings per share. And you can see how they keep growing over time. And that's what Wall Street loves. There are some advantages on a growth company-- the chance to make a lot of money, which gives you more control over your life. You may even be able to go on and do something else, help other people. There's no exquisite timing required. You can buy a [INAUDIBLE] position today and then build that position as you get to know the company better. There's no capital gains tax so your money compounds faster. And then there is the psychological benefit-- the pride of discovery, the joy of ownership, sort of thing. But it's important to point out that growth investing is very difficult. Now it's not as difficult as free climbing at Yosemite or even getting a job here. Just to introduce the price earnings ratio, Amazon's price is about $507. It's going to earn about $4.46 this year. So its price to earnings ratio is 114. If Amazon makes that same level of earnings forever, you'll wait 114 years to get your stock price purchase back. Alphabet's about 20 times earnings. The market's about 21 times earnings and then Apple about 10 times earnings. I introduce the P/E ratio because this chart shows that on the left these are your growth companies. These are the companies that had the highest price earnings ratio. And the companies that we believe are going to have the most growth in front of them, we tend to bid up their price. So they have the lowest subsequent investment returns. And then the companies over on the right, these are your lowest P/E stocks. And the irony is that they had the highest returns. There are three reasons-- three obstacles that confront the growth investor. First of all we buy a company that has poor earnings quality. Second, we buy a company just as a its competitive advantage wanes. And third, we overpay for value that never materializes. So here's our checklist that we're going to work with today. And we're going to start with number one, earnings quality. And to do this I want to introduce generally accepted accounting principals, or GAAP. GAAP is Robert's Rules of Order for America. When you open up an annual report or a 10-K and you look at the financial statements, that's GAAP accounting. And we need GAAP accounting just like motorists need traffic lights. If we didn't have them we'd have chaos. But net income and earnings per share, we think of them as hard numbers or fixed numbers. But that's not the case as I learned 30 years ago when I read this landmark book, "Quality of Earnings," by Thornton O'Glove. He points out in this book that there are many accounting decisions that a CFO can make that influence just how much or how little money a company makes. Bill Ackman, a billionaire hedge fund manager describes, "Quality of Earnings" on his short list of recommended reading. Just as an aside, after I finished my first book and I was looking for people to write an endorsement, the first person I called was Mr. O'Glove. I didn't know him. And we talked and he quickly said yes. And then I found that after that conversation, as I was asking for other endorsements for my book, when I told them that I got the green light from Mr. O'Glove, the endorsements came fast and furious. He wrote just a-- just as a side note, he wrote an op-ed piece for Barron's last fall. And he argues that Berkshire Hathaway should-- it's time for Berkshire to deconglomerate. It's too big and that the pieces are worth more than the sum. So this will be an interesting trend. It's a non-consensus view. This will be something to watch over the next several years. Anyway, other books that I've read which influenced by thinking, the first, "Cash Flow and Security Analysis" by Joshua Livnat and Ken Hackel. And they introduce what's called a free cash flow income statement. And their argument is that the GAAP income statement which we see here in the center, it doesn't tell you how much cash is coming in and out of a company. And so a better measure is one that takes into account investment in fixed and working capital. So let's look at that Alphabet's results for 2015. These results were just posted on Friday. I pulled them off of your website. You made almost $75 billion. So I'm in the GAAP column right now. You made $75 billion of revenue. You had $59 billion of expenses. Your net income is $16.4 billion. And earnings per share almost $22 a share. On a free cash flow basis, we're going to expense investment in fixed capital. Well, what does that mean? That means if you're going out and you're buying rockets, for example or other businesses, or other machinery or equipment that is above your depreciation, that is a use of cash. And depreciation is just your old capital spending that gets written off over time. So in Alphabet's case last year you made an investment of $8.5 billion dollars. So that's a $8.5 billion of cash that's coming out of your corporate checking account that does not appear in the GAAP income statement. Another-- yes. AUDIENCE: [INAUDIBLE]. HEWITT HEISERMAN: It's above depreciation. That's an excellent question. Yes. What you do basically is you take capital spending, you go to the statement of cash flow and take capital spending plus acquisitions minus depreciation. And the reason I include acquisitions because many companies buy other companies because that's a faster way of getting up to speed than building something de novo, where you got to hire people, you got to get-- so it's just a faster way. So $8.6 billion invested in-- $8.5 billion invested in fixed capital. Working capital investment is more modest, $827 million. You have some receivables. You don't have any inventory. So in the big scheme of things, that's just a rounding error. So on a cash basis, if you will, Alphabet last year made $5.96 billion. And one thing I like to look at is I like to see, what's the percentage of free cash flow earnings to GAAP earnings. And here we see that ratio is 37%. So that idea is from this book, "Cash Flow and Security Analysis." I then read another book called, "The Quest for Value," after reading about Coca-Cole. There was a cover story in Fortune magazine, 1995, 1996, and Roberto Goizueta who was the CEO was lauding this EVA approach to capital allocation. And Coke at that time had a 10-year track record of creating some serious amounts of stockholder wealth. This EVA income statement is unique for its own two reasons. Now you'll notice that it does not expense investment in working capital, at least not immediately. What it does expense directly is intangibles like R&D, money that you spend on patents. These would be relevant for your business. Other businesses, it might be the cost of buying subscription lists or marketing efforts, pre-store opening costs. So I want you to compare the difference between the GAAP expense for intangibles and the EVA approach. There's about a $4 billion difference. The EVA approach actually credits you back about $4 billion worth of expenses. Because the mindset here is, we're going to spread those intangibles over their expected useful life. So if you're investing in your people, your processes, or your intellectual property today, we don't expect you to derive value from those outlays today. We think they'll occur in year two, three, four, five, six. So we're going to try to match current sales with current expenses and future sales with future expenses. The other income statement here that's noteworthy is the interest expense or cost of capital which is about $5.7 billion. In the EVA approach, not only is debt treated as an expense but so is stockholder's equity, which you have a lot of. So in the EVA approach, if you buy Alphabet stock or you buy Coca-Cola stock-- Procter & Gamble stock, you have an expected return mindset. You expect to get some return on your stock. And so what the EVA approach tries to do is to capture that cost. Now if accounting's not your thing, the good news is, that's the end of the accounting for today. So I was in a quandary. When do I use the free cash flow income statement and when do I use the EVA income statement? And I built both of these alternate income statements in Excel on my computer, and I had them and I just didn't know which way to go. And then I read a passage from one of Ben Graham's books. Now Ben is the first great investor teacher of the modern age. He came to the United States with his family, graduated from Columbia with three offers to teach at three different departments. His father just passed away. He needed to make some money for his mother and two younger sons so he got a job on Wall Street. And he started making a lot of money pretty quick. And then the depression came along and he was speculating and Ben got wiped out. So he re-jigged his investment methodology and he developed this margin of safety principle, which you're probably familiar with. And we all use margin of safety in our lives. If you have to be at work at-- what time do you have to be at work here? [LAUGHTER] AUDIENCE: Whenever. HEWITT HEISERMAN: Whenever. All right, if you have to be here at whenever, and you know it takes a half hour, you leave 45 minutes before, just in case something happens. So that was his framework for approaching stock selection. Warren Buffett explains margin of safety this way. He says, "you build a bridge that can carry a 30,000 pound truck but then you have a weight limit of 10,000 pounds." Now, Alphabet has a margin of safety. It's a redundancy. It is your data centers that you have around the world. And I assume you have them. You had them as of last week. Right? So it's the same idea. It's a margin of safety. If one data center goes down, you've got others that you can use. Anyway, Ben writes in the, "Intelligent Investor," he says there are two types-- the defensive investor who wants to avoid committing [INAUDIBLE] mistakes, and the enterprising investor who wants to own companies that are more promising than most. So I'm thinking about this. I'm thinking, huh, the defensive investor is kind of like a commercial banker. If it's raining, they want the umbrella that they lent you. They want it back. And they think about corporate profitability kind of like a lemonade stand. Because the way that they're going to make money is if you can repay that loan. And so they're going to focus on how much cash you generate. Their not going to get rich owning your business. So their mindset is very pessimistic, hard money. And that's the way the free cash flow income statement works. And then the other personality type, I think of it as like the way a venture capitalist looks at a business. Here at Alphabet, you have two funding entities, right? They're both early stage. This is according to what I read in the papers. When they sit down and they look at business opportunities, they're creating a pro forma. So they're modeling out revenue going out several years and then they're modeling out expenses. They're going to depreciate or spread over time intangibles and capital spending. But also they want to make a return. Because your stockholders want to make a return. So they're going to have a line in there for the financing that they're providing to this entity. So I want to make a proposal that the GAAP income statement is too, "venture capitalist" for the defensive investor and is too, "commercial banker" for the enterprising investor. And now we're going to return to Alphabet and we're going to look at five years worth of your performance. Now the blue bar, that's your GAAP net income. And that's in the middle because it's kind of in between these two opposing viewpoints about what is corporate profitability. We see a progression of increased positive progression over the last five years. So that's impressive. We have our defensive profits on the left. And you see that beginning in 2013, the gap between GAAP net income has widened. And that's because you're making tremendous investments in fixed capital. Now if you had a lot of debt, if you had a history of write-offs, if your ownership culture-- if I wasn't comfortable with your ownership culture, if I looked at this dichotomy, it would make me somewhat troubled. In Alphabet's case, there's nothing to suggest that these investments in the future are anything to worry about. With the enterprise income statement, we can see that there's a tighter correlation between GAAP profits and enterprise profits. So this gives me comfort that you're making pretty high returns on your earnings. Most of what I'm talking about today, these are ideas that I've collated and thought about from other investors. I guess my one little contribution to this field, such as it is, is what I call the earnings power chart. And so in this approach, we are going to reject the GAAP income statement, because it's like being half pregnant. We're going to focus on the relationship between defense and enterprise in profits. And as you would think, the best-- there are four boxes. And the best box to be is in the upper right box. That means you have defensive profits and enterprise profits. And that's where Alphabet has resided for the last five years. We're now going to step back 15 years to a company called Enron. Enron, in the late 1990s was one of the best performing stocks. It was a stock to last a decade. This is of the 2000s, according to a business publication that's prominent. Its CFO Andy Fastow was named best CFO, chief financial officer. And a lot of people were buying Enron because they thought it was a growth company. Their thesis was based on the income statement. But when we look at their earnings quality through these two alternate metrics, we see that they were in the lower left box every year. So if you were thinking of buying Enron and you ran those numbers through this model, you'd have to reject that thesis. There might have been other reasons to buy the company, but it wasn't because of their quality of their earnings growth. After I finished looking at Enron, I wondered, did either of these two alternate income statements or maybe the earning pie chart tell you in advance that something was wrong with all these other companies? All these other companies here, they all ran into financial difficulty and cost stockholders lots of money. And so I wanted to be like a-- I wanted to see if there is something you could have known before the carnage. And what I found is that often the defensive income statement told you that the company had poor earnings quality and you should go on high alert. And often it was the enterprising income statement. And then sometimes it was both alternate income statements as we see with Enron. AUDIENCE: [INAUDIBLE]. HEWITT HEISERMAN: I didn't do an academic study for that. But what I did do is, I just-- I would say about probably 80%, 85% of the companies that I looked at that ran into financial difficulty, one or both of these alternate income statements told you something was wrong. And you made a case with some of these companies that go bankrupt-- you may not expect that they go bankrupt, but it gives you a starting point to say, OK, what's the relationship between capital spending and depreciation. Or if working capital is a problem, why are their receivables going up? Or why is their inventory going up? If their inventory is going up, maybe consumer preferences have changed, and maybe consumers are moving on to generation five and they no longer want generation four which is all that company may have to offer. So it's really a starting point for further investigation. AUDIENCE: [INAUDIBLE]? HEWITT HEISERMAN: Yep. AUDIENCE: [INAUDIBLE]. HEWITT HEISERMAN: That's a very good ratio to use, and that's faster than building an earnings power chart, because that information is available, I think at Old School Value, for example, which is an excellent website if you're a do it yourself investor. To answer your question, I did not look at these companies in terms of their Altman score because I was trying to learn-- AUDIENCE: [INAUDIBLE]. HEWITT HEISERMAN: Right. Although the Z-score may have picked up-- there's another ratio, the accrual ratio. And the accrual ratio may have picked up similar problems. But the reason why I like seeing the three income statements side by side, because you can just go through each expense, and you look for something that's out of the ordinary. And then you can take that information, you can take like their investment rate in fixed capital and you can compare it to the industry average. So it's really like a jumping off point for to do further research if you see something that's wrong. OK. Enough of failure. Let's look at success. Here is Microsoft during the 1990s. Remember, this company turned a hypothetical $10,000 into a million dollars. This is what we call-- to use Peter Lynch's description, a 100 bagger. What we see here-- I see three things. Number one, the company is in the upper right box, so it has high quality earnings. Number two, it's moving every year in an upper right direction. So I call this an earnings power staircase. This is a sign of profitable growth. Not only is the company getting bigger but it's getting better. And then third, a couple of these years, look at the rate of change from one year-- look at '97 to '98 and then '98 to '99. It's just explosive growth. And this is what Wall Street loves. There is a great book Chris Mayer called, "100 Baggers." If you want to learn more about these kinds of companies I highly recommend this book. It came out last fall. We're now going to look at other companies that had earnings power staircase-like patterns. And we're just going to go through this kind of fast. But I just want you to appreciate that positive trajectory in high quality earnings. [INAUDIBLE] turned $10,000 into $44,000. First Cash Financial, $10,000 into $86,000. Apollo Group, $10 grand into $78,000. Dell Computer, $10 grand into $1.3 million. Cisco Systems, $10 grand into $631,000. Paychex, $10,000 into $257,000. Quality systems, $10,000 into of $70,000. Hansen Natural, $10,000 into $2.6 million. Chico's FAS $10,000 into $73,000. Monster Beverage, $10,000 into $61,000. Monster's interesting because this is the best performing stock of the last 20 years. A hypothetical $10000 investment grew to $10 million. We're going to turn this presentation into a book, and I'll have much more to say about Monster in the book. So if your thesis is growth, if you're a growth investor, I want you to focus on companies that are in the upper right box and that are moving in an upward right direction every year, forging what I call an earnings power staircase. These are the companies that have profitable growth. And the next step is, in our checklist here is competitive advantage. If a company is forging a staircase, it probably has a competitive advantage. There are five types. If you saw Pat Dorsey's presentation here about a year ago-- Pat is the expert on competitive advantage. When he was with Morning Star he and his staff teased out four competitive advantages-- low cost, provider high switching costs, intangibles like brands and patents and that sort of thing, and then network effect, the telephone, Facebook, that sort of thing. And then I add to that list, ecosystems. So if you make a gadget, and the gadget can talk to another gadget that's made by the same company, then you can transfer all that data go as new versions of the gadget come out. That to me is an ecosystem. With a network effect, the more people you have, the more valuable the network. But in theory, in an ecosystem, you really only need one customer. Warren Buffet describes a competitive advantage as a moat. And I bet that Larry and Sergey and Eric probably spend most of their time thinking about this issue. The castle is Alphabet, and the moat is whatever you guys, men and women can come up with that prevents the competition from taking your business. Warren Buffett says that if there are alligators in the moat, that's even better. We're not going to talk about competitive advantage except to say that if you determine that a company has a competitive advantage, and it probably does if it's forging a staircase, then you want to think about the drivers that affect intrinsic value. Companies that have a competitive advantage, they're more valuable than companies that don't have a competitive advantage. If you sell a commodity, you really don't have any pricing power. People will go buy your product from someone else if they can get a better deal. Intrinsic value is our third step. That's what the fair worth of the business is. Morningstar-- they do a lot of great work with estimating companies intrinsic value. They project that the business-- Alphabet's worth $755 a share. The stock price as of last week was $682. So the price to intrinsic value is 90%. If you buy Alphabet stock today, you're paying $0.90 cents for a dollar's worth of value. If you knew that, for whatever reason, the price intrinsic value was going to go down to 75%, then you would wait because then you'd get even more value for your money. Professor [INAUDIBLE] spoke to your group. And if you want to learn more about valuation, check out his presentation which is excellent. It's getting harder to estimate a company's intrinsic value because if you have to make assumptions about how long the business is going to last. And as this research shows, in five years from today, 32% of US public companies will be out of business. They'll be either acquired by other companies or they'll just go bankrupt. Versus 50 years ago, it was only 5%. So the rate of change is accelerating, and for better or for worse, Alphabet is one of the prime disruptors. One item I want to point out that is something to watch is that your incremental capital is trending down. You're making bets that are outside your core business. Hopefully those bets will pay off and then that trend will reverse. This will be something to watch. To learn more about intrinsic value there's a great resource, Valuentum Securities which I subscribe to and I highly recommend. And I mentioned earlier, Old School Value which I also subscribe to. They give you 10 years worth of financial statements. Just type in the symbol and the information's right there and they have a lot of pre-programmed valuation models. So you don't have to build the thing from scratch and spend a couple of weeks doing that. All the information's right at your fingertips. Now I mentioned that Ben Graham-- yes. AUDIENCE: [INAUDIBLE]? MALE SPEAKER: Yeah, he will be. HEWITT HEISERMAN: Yep. I've mentioned that Ben was affected by the depression. And so he took a hard money approach to buying stocks. So his method was what he called-- this is after he figured out a new approach. He would buy companies that were selling at 2/3 of their net working capital. So taking your balance sheet from December 31, 2015. He gave 100% for your cash. He'd give you a 75% for your receivables. You don't have any inventory. And then he'd subtract all your liabilities. And then he'd take your net working capital, he'd multiply that by 66% of that. And then that would leave you $36 billion. He would pay $36 billion for the business. You've got 745 million shares outstanding, so he'd paid $45. Is that right? $48 for Google. All right. That's what he would buy it for. All right. Now we're at step four, position sizing. Position sizing is simply, what percentage of your portfolio or your capital are you going to put into any single position? Now it stands to reason that if you have an edge, then you should exploit it. And this is what Warren Buffett did after the famous salad oil scandal in 1963. It knocked shares of American Express down. Mr. Buffet determined that American Express' franchise was intact, and he put 40% of the partnerships funds into American Express and it then went up five-fold in five years. You really have to be honest with yourself though in terms of whether or not you have an edge. There are four types-- information, analytic, behavioral, and structural. You also want to ask yourself, what's the consequence if I am wrong, and can I afford that consequence? My advice is, if you don't have an edge, you start small, especially with these growth companies because we see how core the subsequent investment returns are. And then build your position over time as you get to know the company better. You may get a better entry point in terms of price to intrinsic value. And absolutely positively have a sell strategy, which is something we'll cover here in a short moment. For men especially, you've got to guard against overconfidence. And there are people that have gotten PhD's on this topic. I'm not going to talk about it at length. You can look into it if you want. But Curt Schilling-- we live in Boston. Curt Schilling of the famous bloody sock, retired, he was into games and started a business, 38 Studios. He put his entire $50 million net worth into the business, and then business went bankrupt. Other examples of overconfidence include the Hunt brothers with silver in the 1970s and then long-term capital management. I had my own overconfidence story. I invested in China Media Express in 2011. It seemingly passed the three checklist items that we've just discussed-- high quality earnings, competitive advantage, and it was cheap. It was selling at eight times earnings, had $200 million of cash, no debt, audited financials by Deloitte. Hank Greenberg, who had built AIG into one the preeminent insurance companies, he had put $80 million into China Media Express. And one of his colleagues was on the board. But, alas, China Media Express was a fraud. There was no $200 million. So after the grieving process was over, I determined that I was going to turn lemons into lemonade. And I did a post-mortem or in this case an autopsy of what I did wrong and identified three errors, two of which we're going to get to shortly. And I realized that I never wanted to be in a position where I was down 25% on a portfolio. So this leads to position size. There is a study by Dr. Van Tharp of people-- that they all get a hypothetical $100,000. They all get the same trades. The same number of winning stocks, the same number of losing stocks, both in terms of frequency and magnitude. And yet, 50 simulated trades later, the ending balance of capital ranges from completely wipe out to $13 million. And Dr. Thorpe says the reason for this is position sizing and in psychology.
